questions.question: How do you approach a Ruby coding interview round?
questions.title: Approaching the Coding Round
questions.direct_answer: In a coding round you solve a problem live. The process: 1) clarify the problem (ask about input, edge cases, expected output), 2) work an example by hand, 3) state the approach and its complexity (say it's O(n) with a hash), 4) write clean code using Ruby idioms (each/map, a hash, not a C-style index loop), 5) trace it on an example, 6) discuss edge cases (empty, nil, duplicates). Talk while you code so the interviewer follows your thinking. Pick the simple correct approach first; optimize only if asked. Use Ruby's strengths (Enumerable, hash defaults) to write short, readable code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you follow the process (clarify, example, approach+complexity, code, trace, edge cases) and talk while coding.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Jumping to code before clarifying, or silent coding (interviewer can't follow your thinking).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify -> example -> approach + complexity -> code (idiomatic Ruby) -> trace -> edge cases. Talk while coding; correct before optimal.

sections.title: A Process, Not Just Code
sections.content: In a coding round you solve a problem live. The process: one, clarify the problem — ask about the input, the edge cases, and the expected output. Two, work an example by hand so you understand the transformation. Three, state the approach and its complexity — say it's O(n) with a hash. Four, write clean code using Ruby idioms like each and map, a hash, not a C-style index loop. Five, trace it on an example out loud. Six, discuss edge cases — empty, nil, duplicates. Talk while you code so the interviewer follows your thinking. Pick the simple correct approach first and optimize only if asked. Use Ruby's strengths — Enumerable, hash defaults — to write short, readable code.

sections.title: The Coding-Round Process
sections.content:
Clarify, example, approach+complexity, code, trace, edge cases.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Cl[clarify] --> Ex[example by hand]
  Ex --> Ap[approach + O\(\)]
  Ap --> Co[code in Ruby]
  Co --> Tr[trace on example]
  Tr --> Ed[edge cases]
```

sections.title: A coding-round flow
sections.content:
```ruby
# Q: 'Return the first duplicate in an array.'

# 1) Clarify: 'first by index? any duplicate? what if none?' -> first by index; nil if none.
# 2) Example: [4, 3, 2, 3, 4] -> 3 (3 appears again at index 3, before 4's repeat)
# 3) Approach: walk once, use a seen set; O(n) time, O(n) space.
# 4) Code:
def first_duplicate(arr)
  seen = {}
  arr.each do |x|
    return x if seen[x]
    seen[x] = true
  end
  nil
end
# 5) Trace on [4,3,2,3,4]: seen={}, x=4->{4}, x=3->{4,3}, x=2->{4,3,2}, x=3 -> seen[3] -> return 3. OK.
# 6) Edge cases: [], no dup (nil), all same ([5,5] -> 5).
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Jumping to code before clarifying — you may solve the wrong problem.
Silent coding — the interviewer can't follow your thinking; talk through it.
Optimizing before a correct solution exists — get correct first, optimize if asked.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: In a coding round: clarify, example, approach + complexity, code, trace, edge cases.
Talk while you code so the interviewer follows your thinking.
Use Ruby idioms (each/map, a hash, hash defaults) over C-style index loops.
Pick the simple correct approach first; optimize only if asked.
Always discuss edge cases (empty, nil, duplicates) at the end.
